messages.author: 6367030a31173e4d
messages.subject: Sampling level required for MRDS
parts:
Hello again,

 

Does anybody know if a recommended sample size or proportion of primary observer detections exists that are required for MRDS?  That is, how many duplicate (primary & independent observer) detections are necessary to generate absolute abundance estimates? I’m in a situation where I have a ~1.5 year dataset from line-transect surveys which I will continue for another six months. Due to limited observer availability in all monthly surveys bar one, no independent observers were present. So I have just a handful of duplicate detections. I may have the opportunity to have more observers in the next six months but wonder if it is too late and therefore unnecessary to include independent observers. I have 55 objects in 1.5 years to give you an idea of detection rate, which will vary greatly seasonally, although we are approaching peak season so good opportunities for higher detection rates.  

 

I’ve been searching the literature including the Distance Sampling books but not found anything yet.

 

Many thanks in advance,

 

Gemma Veneruso

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Sampling level required for MRDS
parts:
Gemma

There is no simple formula to answer the sample size question you ask.  Recognize you are on the low end of fitting a detection function in conventional terms with the numbers of detections you note (if they were to have come from a single observer).  Indeed you are fitting more than a single detection function when performing double observer analysis.  Under the "io" (independent observer) configuration, you will be fitting a curve to the duplicates, so you might consider striving for >50 duplicates to perform that fitting.

As to whether to not seek double observer data for your current study given your present situation, recognise information learned from additional double observer configuration protocol will aide in future ventures to help with questions such as 'how do we do a better job of determining when we have duplicate sightings' (even if the current study falls into the 'pilot study' category).
